misconceptions.statement: To convert any pm time to 24-hour time, add 12 to the hour, so 12:30 pm is 24:30.
misconceptions.why: The add-12 rule is learnt for 1 pm to 11 pm and applied blindly to 12 pm.
misconceptions.fix: 12 pm (noon) stays 12:xx. Add 12 only for hours from 1 pm to 11 pm.

probe.question: Write 12:30 pm in 24-hour time.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule works for every case without exceptions

misconceptions.statement: In the 24-hour clock, 1 am is written 13:00 and 1 pm is written 01:00.
misconceptions.why: Students remember that 13 relates to 1 but mix up which half of the day is which.
misconceptions.fix: Morning hours stay the same (1 am = 01:00). Afternoon hours are 12 more (1 pm = 13:00).

probe.question: Write 1 pm in 24-hour time.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar looking labels mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: 12 am is noon and 12 pm is midnight.
misconceptions.why: am sounds like 'morning' and 12 feels like the middle of the day, and the labels ante/post meridiem are not understood.
misconceptions.fix: 12 pm is noon, 12 am is midnight, the start of a new day (00:00).

probe.question: A shop opens at 12 am. Is it open in the afternoon or in the middle of the night?
probe.wrong_answer: It opens at noon in the afternoon.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom studies of children's difficulties with am/pm and 12-hour clock conventions

misconceptions.statement: Midnight belongs to the day that is ending, so 00:00 of Tuesday is the same moment as the end of Tuesday.
misconceptions.why: Night feels like a continuation of the evening, so students attach midnight to the previous day.
misconceptions.fix: 00:00 is the start of the new day. The end of Tuesday is 24:00, which is the same moment as 00:00 on Wednesday.

probe.question: A train leaves at 23:30 on Monday and the journey takes 1 hour. Which day does it arrive?

misconceptions.root_belief: events stay in the same group until something visible changes

misconceptions.statement: 1 hour is 100 minutes, so 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.30 hours and 2.5 hours means 2 hours 5 minutes.
misconceptions.why: Decimal place value is applied to a base-60 system.
misconceptions.fix: 1 hour is 60 minutes. 2.5 hours is 2 hours 30 minutes, and 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.5 hours, not 2.30.

probe.question: How many minutes are in 2.5 hours?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's difficulties with non-decimal (sexagesimal) units of time

misconceptions.statement: When subtracting times, borrowing 1 hour gives 10 extra minutes, like borrowing in ordinary subtraction.
misconceptions.why: The borrowing procedure from decimal subtraction is repeated mechanically.
misconceptions.fix: Borrowing 1 hour gives 60 minutes, so 3:20 - 1:45 is 2 hours 80 minutes - 1 hour 45 minutes = 1 hour 35 minutes.

probe.question: Find 3 h 20 min - 1 h 45 min.
probe.wrong_answer: 1 h 35 min computed as 2 h 30 min - 1 h 45 min = 0 h 45 min

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of errors in time subtraction and regrouping in non-decimal units

misconceptions.statement: 2 h 45 min + 1 h 30 min = 3 h 75 min, and that is the final answer.
misconceptions.why: Students add columns separately and do not realise minutes cannot exceed 59 in standard form.
misconceptions.fix: 75 minutes is 1 hour 15 minutes, so the sum is 4 h 15 min.

probe.question: Add 2 h 45 min and 1 h 30 min.

misconceptions.root_belief: digits in separate columns can be treated independently
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's errors with time addition

misconceptions.statement: Adding 50 minutes to 4:30 gives 4:80.
misconceptions.why: The clock face is thought of as a number line that continues past 60.
misconceptions.fix: After 4:59 the clock goes to 5:00. 4:30 + 50 minutes = 5:20.

probe.question: What time is it 50 minutes after 4:30?

misconceptions.root_belief: numbers keep counting up with no limit

misconceptions.statement: Elapsed time is found by subtracting the smaller number from the larger one, whichever time is first.
misconceptions.why: Students treat times as plain numbers and subtract the clock digits in the easiest direction.
misconceptions.fix: Elapsed time is finish time minus start time. When the clock passes 12 or midnight, count in parts or use the 24-hour clock.

probe.question: A film starts at 9:40 and ends at 11:15. How long is it?
probe.wrong_answer: 2 hours 35 minutes (11-9 hours and 40-15 minutes added)

misconceptions.root_belief: smaller from larger always gives the answer
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's elapsed-time reasoning errors

misconceptions.statement: A journey from 10 pm to 4 am takes 4 - 10 = 6 hours.
misconceptions.why: Students subtract the hour numbers ignoring the passing of midnight.
misconceptions.fix: From 10 pm to midnight is 2 hours and midnight to 4 am is 4 hours, so the total is 6 hours; students must count through midnight, not just subtract numbers and always get the right answer by luck.

probe.question: A train leaves at 9 pm and arrives at 3 am. How long is the journey?
probe.wrong_answer: 6 hours is wrong since 3 - 9 = -6, so 6 hours gone the other way, i.e. 18 hours

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Time from 11 am to 2 pm is 9 hours because 11 - 2 = 9.
misconceptions.why: The am/pm change is ignored and the hour digits are subtracted in the 12-hour clock.
misconceptions.fix: 11 am to 12 noon is 1 hour, and 12 noon to 2 pm is 2 hours, so the total is 3 hours. Converting to 14:00 - 11:00 also gives 3 hours.

probe.question: How long is it from 11 am to 2 pm?

misconceptions.root_belief: digits can be subtracted without checking what they mean
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's errors when time intervals cross noon

misconceptions.statement: Every 4th year is a leap year, so 1900 and 2100 are leap years.
misconceptions.why: The divisible-by-4 rule is taught first and the century exception is forgotten.
misconceptions.fix: A century year (like 1900 or 2100) is a leap year only if divisible by 400. So 1900 and 2100 are not leap years, but 2000 is.

probe.question: Is 2100 a leap year?

misconceptions.root_belief: a simple rule has no exceptions
misconceptions.source_hint: teacher reports and textbook error analyses on leap year rule

misconceptions.statement: A century year is a leap year only if it is divisible by 100.
misconceptions.why: Students mix the numbers 4, 100 and 400 from the rule.
misconceptions.fix: Century years are divisible by 100 by definition. They are leap years only when divisible by 400. So 1600 and 2000 are leap, 1700 is not.

probe.question: Is 1700 a leap year?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar numbers in a rule are interchangeable

misconceptions.statement: A leap year has an extra day in every month of February and the year has 366 days because every month gets longer.
misconceptions.why: The idea of an extra day is blurred with the idea of a longer year.
misconceptions.fix: Only February gets an extra day (29 days) in a leap year. The year has 366 days.

probe.question: How many days are in March of a leap year?

misconceptions.root_belief: a change affects everything nearby

misconceptions.statement: The number of days from 5 March to 20 March is 16 because you count both the first and last day.
misconceptions.why: Counting objects in a list includes both ends, and students apply this to date differences.
misconceptions.fix: Days from 5 March to 20 March is 20 - 5 = 15. Count both ends only if the question says 'including both days'.

probe.question: How many days from 5 March to 20 March?

misconceptions.root_belief: counting endpoints always includes both ends
misconceptions.source_hint: fence-post / off-by-one error research in interval counting

misconceptions.statement: Days between two dates in different months are found by just subtracting the day numbers, so 25 January to 5 February is 20 days.
misconceptions.why: Students subtract 25 from 5 and flip it to 20 ignoring the month length.
misconceptions.fix: Count the days left in January (31 - 25 = 6) and add 5, giving 11 days.

probe.question: How many days from 25 January to 5 February?

misconceptions.root_belief: smaller from larger always gives the answer

misconceptions.statement: Months with 30 days and 31 days alternate all year, so August has 30 days.
misconceptions.why: The alternate pattern works from January to July and is overextended.
misconceptions.fix: July and August both have 31 days. February has 28 or 29, and April, June, September, November have 30.

probe.question: How many days does August have?

misconceptions.root_belief: a pattern continues forever once it starts

misconceptions.statement: The minute hand turns 1 degree for each minute, so at 20 minutes it is 20 degrees from 12.
misconceptions.why: Minute marks are confused with degree marks.
misconceptions.fix: The minute hand makes 360 degrees in 60 minutes, so 6 degrees per minute. At 20 minutes it is 120 degrees from 12.

probe.question: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 20 minutes?

misconceptions.root_belief: one unit of a scale equals one unit of another
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' angle concept and clock-angle problems

misconceptions.statement: The hour hand stays exactly on the hour mark until the next hour starts, so at 3:30 the angle between hands is 180 - 90 = 90 degrees.
misconceptions.why: Students think the hour hand jumps rather than moves continuously.
misconceptions.fix: The hour hand moves 0.5 degrees per minute. At 3:30 it is at 105 degrees and the minute hand at 180, so the angle is 75 degrees.

probe.question: What is the angle between the hands at 3:30?

misconceptions.root_belief: what moves slowly does not move
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' reasoning on clock-hand angle problems

misconceptions.statement: At 6 o'clock the angle between the hands is 90 degrees, as 6 is a quarter-turn.
misconceptions.why: Students link 3 and 9 with right angles and are unsure which clock positions give which angles.
misconceptions.fix: At 6 o'clock the hands point opposite, 6 x 30 = 180 degrees. The angle is 90 degrees at 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock.

probe.question: What is the angle between the hands at 6 o'clock?

misconceptions.root_belief: the first example you learnt is the general case

misconceptions.statement: Time zones differ because places are of different heights or distances from the Sun, so there is no pattern in hours.
misconceptions.why: Time difference is linked to weather or sunlight instead of the Earth's rotation.
misconceptions.fix: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, 15 degrees an hour, so each 15 degrees of longitude changes local time by 1 hour.

probe.question: Two cities are 30 degrees of longitude apart. What is the time difference?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot be found, it depends on their distance from the Sun.

misconceptions.root_belief: nearby visible things cause effects directly
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about day, night and time around the Earth

misconceptions.statement: Places to the west of India are ahead of Indian time, so London is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the direction of the Sun's apparent motion with the direction of time.
misconceptions.fix: The Sun rises first in the east, so places east are ahead. London is 5 h 30 min behind India.

probe.question: It is 3 pm in India. What time is it in London (no daylight saving)?

misconceptions.root_belief: adding is the natural direction to change a quantity
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of misconceptions in time-zone calculations and sign of the time difference

misconceptions.statement: All of India's neighbours and the whole world show the same time because the clock is one global system.
misconceptions.why: Everyday life uses one clock locally, so students assume one time is shared everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: Local time depends on longitude. India uses one standard time (IST), but other countries are ahead or behind.

probe.question: It is noon in India. Is it also noon in Japan?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, noon everywhere at the same instant.

misconceptions.root_belief: what I experience is the same for everyone
